blocks.md:
An operating system runs each program in a **process**. Inside a process, independent parts can run at the same time as **threads**. Splitting work across threads can make a program faster on multi-core machines, or keep it responsive while it waits. It also brings classic problems:

- **Race conditions**: threads access data in an inconsistent order.
- **Deadlocks**: two threads each wait for the other, forever.
- **Heisenbugs**: bugs that happen only sometimes and vanish when you look.

Rust's ownership and type system turn many of these into **compile-time errors**. The Rust community calls this **fearless concurrency**: you can refactor concurrent code and the compiler tells you when you break something.

blocks.title: Spawning a thread
blocks.md: `std::thread::spawn` takes a closure and runs it on a new thread. Rust uses **1:1** threads: one operating-system thread per language thread.

blocks.explain: Run it a few times: the two threads take turns in a different order each time, decided by the operating system's scheduler. And the spawned thread **does not finish**: when `main` returns, the whole process ends, and every other thread is stopped.

blocks.title: Waiting with join
blocks.md: `spawn` returns a **`JoinHandle<T>`**. Calling **`.join()`** on it blocks the current thread until that thread finishes. Where you call it matters:

blocks.output:
main keeps working while the sum runs...
sum = 500000500000
blocks.explain: `join` returns `Result<T, _>`: `Ok` with the closure's return value, or `Err` if the thread panicked. A panic in a spawned thread does not crash the others; `join` is where you find out about it (*Programming Rust*).

blocks.title: move closures and threads
blocks.md: A thread's closure often needs data from the spawning thread. It must **own** that data, because Rust cannot know how long the thread will run:

blocks.explain: If this compiled, `main` could `drop(v)` while the thread still uses it. With `move`, the vector moves into the thread, and `main` can no longer touch it: the compiler then rejects `drop(v)` instead.

blocks.title: Scoped threads can borrow
blocks.md: `move` is not always what you want: sometimes several threads should **read** the same local data, and you will wait for all of them anyway. **`thread::scope`** guarantees that every thread spawned inside it is joined before the scope returns, so those threads may borrow local variables:

blocks.explain: This is **fork-join parallelism** (*Programming Rust*): split the work, run the parts in parallel, join the results. No `move`, no cloning, no `Arc`; the borrow checker knows the threads end inside the scope.

blocks.title: What a thread costs (Rust in Action)
blocks.md: Spawning an OS thread takes microseconds and reserves its own stack (2 MiB by default for Rust threads). *Rust in Action* measures that a few threads are almost free, but thousands start to slow the whole program, and spinning in a loop wastes CPU that `thread::sleep` or `thread::yield_now` would give back. For many small tasks, use a thread pool (chapter 25) or async (chapter 17).

blocks.title: Fork-join helpers
blocks.goal: Split work across threads, both with move and with scoped threads, and handle a panicking thread.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub fn parallel_sum(data: &[u64], parts: usize) -> u64`: split `data` into `parts` chunks (use `chunks` with a size of `ceil(len / parts)`, at least 1) and sum each chunk on its own **scoped** thread. Empty data gives 0.
- `pub fn map_in_threads(inputs: Vec<String>, f: fn(&str) -> String) -> Vec<String>`: one spawned thread per input (with `move`), results in the input order.
- `pub fn run_safely(job: fn() -> i32) -> Result<i32, String>`: run `job` on a thread; if it panicked, return `Err("job panicked")`.
hints: `thread::scope(|s| { let handles: Vec<_> = data.chunks(size).map(|c| s.spawn(move || c.iter().sum::<u64>())).collect(); handles.into_iter().map(|h| h.join().unwrap()).sum() })`
`fn` pointers are `Copy` and `Send`, so `f` can be moved into many threads.
blocks.solution_explain: Collecting the handles into a vector **before** joining is essential: joining inside the same `map` would wait for each thread before starting the next, making the code sequential. In `parallel_sum`, `move` copies the chunk reference `c` into the closure; the scope lets that borrow of `data` be used across threads.

questions.q: What happens to spawned threads when main returns?
options: They are stopped, whether finished or not

questions.q: What does `handle.join()` return if the thread panicked?
questions.explanation: Panics are reported through join's Result.

questions.q: Why must closures passed to thread::spawn usually be `move`?
options: The thread may outlive the variables it borrows
Every thread spawned in it is joined before the scope ends, so they may borrow locals
Only one thread runs at a time

questions.q: Spawning and joining inside the same loop iteration makes the work...
questions.explanation: Spawn them all first, then join.

points: `thread::spawn(closure)` starts a thread; its `JoinHandle` lets you `join` and get the return value.
When `main` ends, all threads end; join the ones you need.
Use `move` to give a thread ownership of its data.
`thread::scope` lets threads borrow local data, because they are joined before the scope ends.
Spawn everything first, then join, or the work runs one after another.

terms.def: An independently scheduled sequence of execution inside a process.
The value returned by thread::spawn; join waits for the thread and returns its result.
A bug where the result depends on the timing of threads accessing shared data.
Threads waiting for each other forever.
A thread spawned with thread::scope, guaranteed to finish before the scope ends, so it can borrow locals.
Splitting work into parts, running them in parallel, and joining the results.
